title: How chimps teach their kids tool tricks
gist: A Frontiers in Psychology paper based on eight years of camera-trap footage at Senegal's Dindefelo Community Nature Reserve documents 33 chimpanzee tool transfers, mostly adult females handing tools to infants, and argues this constitutes active teaching rather than passive observational learning. The finding matters because teaching is thought to evolve specifically for skills too complex to acquire through observation alone.

insights.claim: Researchers analyzing chimpanzee camera-trap footage argue that tool and food transfer from experienced individuals is a form of teaching alongside observation and supervised practice, with mothers acting as the main models and teachers for young chimpanzees.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Pushes the boundary of documented non-human teaching, strengthening the case for cultural transmission as a driver of cognitive evolution.
insights.quote: Tool transfers thus appear to be a form of teaching, together with observation and supervised practice. It appears that mothers are the main models and teachers for young chimpanzees in this manner.

insights.claim: Teaching is defined in this research as requiring an active role from the teacher who must modify their own behavior to facilitate transmission, and is thought to have evolved specifically to transfer information too complex for individual or observational learning.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: This definition is the testable criterion that separates genuine teaching claims from anthropomorphic over-reading in animal cognition studies.
insights.quote: It requires an active role from the teacher, who must modify their behavior to facilitate the transmission of information to the learner
insights.locator: Teaching is one of the strategies that chimpanzees use

insights.claim: Between 2017 and 2025 researchers collected nearly 15 hours of camera-trap video from 14 locations in the Dindefelo Community Nature Reserve in Senegal's Kedougou region, yielding 33 instances of tool transfer, three attempted transfers, and four baobab fruit transfers.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Eight years of fieldwork for 15 hours of usable footage shows how thin the evidence base for wild primate cognition still is — treat single-study conclusions cautiously.
insights.locator: Between 2017 and 2025, the authors collected observational data

insights.claim: Of the documented chimpanzee tool transfers, 58 percent occurred during ant dipping, 30 percent during algae fishing, and 12 percent during termite fishing, concentrating the behavior in the hardest-to-access food extraction tasks.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Transfer clusters where the skill is hardest, consistent with the theory that teaching evolves for complex skills rather than being general-purpose.

insights.claim: Original tool holders were usually adults (58 percent) and predominantly female, recipients were most often infants (42 percent), about 30 percent of transfers were mother-to-offspring, and in all but one case the recipient initiated the voluntary transfer.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Recipient-initiated transfer complicates the pure teaching story — it looks as much like tolerated begging as like deliberate instruction.
insights.locator: The original tool holders were usually adults

insights.claim: Not all transfers were cooperative: some chimps simply stole tools or fruit, prompting either a retaliatory strike from the original holder or the holder grabbing the item back.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Theft cases are the natural control condition that keeps the teaching interpretation honest.

insights.claim: In February 2018 footage, an adult female chimp named Soukki dipped a twig into an ant nest, left it in place, brought over her infant Saïsaï who pulled out the twig and ate the ants — and a later recording showed Saïsaï fully mimicking the ant-dipping behavior.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A before-and-after sequence on an identified individual is the strongest single piece of evidence that transfer causes skill acquisition rather than merely accompanying it.

insights.claim: In December 2021 footage, a male juvenile chimp physically guided infant Fotti's hand to demonstrate pounding a baobab fruit against a rocky outcrop after Fotti's own attempts failed, and Fotti then repeated the motion and broke the fruit open.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Hand-guiding by a non-mother juvenile suggests the teaching role is not exclusively maternal, widening the transmission network.

insights.claim: Wild bird tool use has been observed only in corvids, while the 2012 captive cockatoo Figaro spontaneously performed multi-step tool processing never seen in that species in the wild, showing captivity can reveal latent capabilities absent from field observation.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Field-observation-only surveys systematically understate animal cognitive capacity, a sampling bias worth applying to any 'only humans can' claim.

insights.claim: A Swiss brown cow in Austria named Veronika was documented picking up random sticks to scratch herself, a form of multipurpose tool use suggesting scientists have underestimated bovine cognitive capabilities.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Tool use appearing in a domesticated livestock species undercuts the assumption that it tracks phylogenetic closeness to primates.
insights.quote: It’s a form of multipurpose tool use and suggests that the cognitive capabilities of cows have been underestimated by scientists.

insights.claim: Chimpanzee mirror neurons fire in response to both object-directed (transitive) and non-object-directed (intransitive) actions much like human mirror neurons, which the authors cite as the neural basis making chimps ideal subjects for studying social learning in tool transfer.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A shared neural substrate for imitation is the mechanism that links the behavioral observation to a general theory of cultural learning.
insights.locator: This latest study focuses specifically on tool transfer
